title: HTTP methods, status codes and headers
description: Understand HTTP verbs, status code families, and the most important request and response headers used in web development.

data.text: HTTP methods, status codes, and headers are the vocabulary of the web. Together they describe what a client wants, what happened, and how the result should be handled. Mastering these makes debugging, API design, and security configuration much easier.
Methods describe the action the client wants to perform. The most common are safe methods that do not change server state, and unsafe methods that do.

data.title: Safe and idempotent explained
data.text: Safe means the method should not change server data. Idempotent means making the same request multiple times has the same effect as making it once. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is generally not.
Status codes are grouped by their first digit. Each family tells you something broad about what happened, while the specific code gives the exact outcome.

data.title: Status code families
items: 2xx Success: action was received, understood, and accepted
3xx Redirection: further action must be taken to complete the request
4xx Client Error: the request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled
5xx Server Error: the server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request

data.title: 4xx vs 5xx
data.text: A 4xx means the client sent something wrong. A 5xx means the server itself failed. Client-side code should not retry 4xx errors without changing the request. 5xx errors are sometimes worth retrying.
Headers carry metadata that changes how requests are sent, cached, or processed. Some control caching, others describe content, and others authenticate the caller.

cards.title: Request headers
cards.description: Sent by the client to describe what it wants or who it is.
items: Host: the domain and optional port
Authorization: bearer token or basic credentials
Content-Type: format of the request body
Accept: response formats the client can handle
Cookie: stored cookies for the domain

cards.title: Response headers
cards.description: Sent by the server to describe the result and how to handle it.
items: Content-Type: format of the response body
Set-Cookie: instructs browser to store a cookie

data.title: Cache-Control matters
data.text: A missing or misconfigured Cache-Control header often causes unnecessary network traffic. Browsers default to revalidating everything unless told otherwise.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Methods describe intent: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, DELETE removes.
Status code families give immediate context: 2xx is success, 4xx is client error, 5xx is server error.
Headers control caching, authentication, content negotiation, and CORS.
Reading status codes and headers correctly is essential for debugging APIs.
data.takeaway: Treat HTTP methods, status codes, and headers as a contract between client and server. When either side violates that contract, failures are cryptic.

items.question: Why do some APIs use POST for everything?
items.answer: POST is universally supported and easy to use with HTML forms. However, using proper methods improves caching, debugging, and API documentation.

items.question: What is the difference between 301 and 302?
items.answer: 301 is a permanent redirect; browsers and search engines update their stored URLs. 302 is temporary; the original URL is expected to return.

items.question: When should I use 304 Not Modified?
items.answer: You do not send 304 directly; the server sends it in response to a conditional request (with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since) when the cached copy is still fresh.

data.text: HTTP status codes are the standardized language of the web. Learn them, and debugging becomes a conversation instead of a mystery.
